title: Creative Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Education
venue: Palgrave Studies in Creativity and Culture (Springer/Palgrave Macmillan)
extended_summary:
This book-length edited volume examines how artificial intelligence, especially generative AI and other AI tools, can be integrated into education with a focus on creativity, ethics, and human–AI collaboration. The opening chapter frames AI in education as both an opportunity and a challenge: it can support personalised learning, creative pedagogies, and hybrid intelligence, but it also raises concerns about privacy, bias, agency, and techno-solutionist assumptions about educational change.

The volume is organised into three parts. The first develops a theoretical account of creative engagement with AI and proposes a six-level model ranging from passive consumption of AI-generated content to expansive learning supported by AI. The second part presents concrete examples for K-12 education, including perspectives from educators and learners on AI use in school contexts. The third part extends the discussion to higher education and other educational settings, such as teacher education, professional training, games, and chatbots. Across these chapters, the book argues that AI should be used to augment, not replace, human agency and creativity.

Because the text provided is primarily introductory and chapter-level framing rather than an empirical study, the main conclusion is conceptual: effective use of AI in education requires critical, ethical, and learner-centred implementation. The editors emphasise that educators and learners need AI literacy and opportunities to co-design human–AI learning activities so that AI supports problem-solving, creativity, and expansive learning rather than narrowing pedagogy or shifting control away from teachers and students.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: Intelligent tutoring systems are AI-driven educational systems that provide individualized instruction, guidance, and feedback based on learner responses and performance.
identified_tools.use_case: The chapter is a literature review of AI in education that discusses ITS as a common class of AI tools in education, especially as the dominant form of current AI use at the second level of the chapter’s creative engagement model.

findings.finding_summary: The review characterizes ITS as the main AI application currently used in education, especially at the 'interactive consumer' level of the model. It notes that ITS can support learning by providing individualized assistance and feedback, but the chapter does not report quantitative effect sizes or sample sizes for ITS outcomes.
findings.measure: Individualized tutoring / learner support in education

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI refers to AI systems that produce text, images, or other content in response to prompts, including large language models and AI chatbots.
identified_tools.use_case: The chapter discusses generative AI tools such as ChatGPT as part of the broader AI-in-education landscape, emphasizing their potential for human-AI collaboration, creative pedagogy, and learner support rather than evaluating a single product.

findings.finding_summary: The chapter says generative AI may be used for composing written essays and other creative writing tasks, suggesting possible support for literacy-related production. It also emphasizes concerns about access, bias, privacy, and responsible use; however, it does not provide outcome data, effect sizes, or sample sizes.
findings.measure: Writing / essay composition and broader literacy-related support

quality_tier_rationale: This is a chapter introduction/literature-review-style overview rather than an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It discusses AI categories and conceptual models, but reports no study design, effect sizes, or sample sizes for tool outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The chapter argues that AI and generative AI may influence learning and literacy through personalization, feedback, and content generation, but provides no empirical effect estimates. Any impact is therefore theoretical and unclear rather than demonstrated.
